text: Last lesson made the case for templating instead of copy-pasted YAML. Now let's actually build the chart. We'll scaffold it, read every file Helm generates, and end up with a real deployment template pulling its values from a shared set of defaults.

helm create myapp generates this exact layout. Chart.yaml is the chart's own manifest. values.yaml holds the defaults every template reads from. The templates folder holds your actual Kubernetes manifests, written with placeholders instead of hardcoded values. And underscore helpers dot t p l defines reusable named templates, so you're not retyping the same labeling logic in five different files.

Chart.yaml carries two separate version numbers, and this trips people up constantly. Version is the chart's own version — bump it when you change a template or a default. appVersion is the version of the application the chart points at by default — bump it when you ship a new image tag. They move independently, on purpose.

Here's a real deployment template. include myapp dot fullname calls a named helper instead of repeating that naming logic. replicas and the image tag both come straight from Values. And toYaml piped through nindent takes an entire structured block out of values.yaml — like resource requests and limits — and drops it into the manifest at the correct indentation, instead of hardcoding every field by hand.

Before any of this touches a real cluster, two commands catch problems early. helm lint checks the chart's structure and flags missing required values. helm template renders the exact YAML helm install would produce, with zero cluster interaction, so you can read the final output and confirm it's right first.

That's a complete, working chart for one application — scaffolded, correctly versioned, templated instead of hardcoded, and checked before it ever reaches a cluster. Next lesson, we give it separate values files for dev, staging, and production — the same pattern Terraform used for variable files per workspace, now applied to Kubernetes manifests instead of infrastructure.
